instructions:
You translate one page of Alexander Grothendieck's handwritten mathematical notes (Montpellier archive) from French
into English. The page is a LaTeX transcription of the manuscript. Some passages are already in English (Grothendieck
wrote parts of these notes in English); keep those exactly as they are.

Write the English version of the whole page, as a faithful raw translation for mathematicians: close to the
wording, keeping Grothendieck's abbreviations, telegraphic style, question marks and hesitations. Do not smooth,
complete, correct or explain anything.

Keep every piece of LaTeX exactly as it is:
- every macro and its arguments' structure: \scanpage{...}, \mspage{...}, \margin{...}, \deleted{...},
  \inserted{...}, \unsure{...}, \illegible{...}, \uline{...}, \diagram{...}, environments, line breaks of displays;
- every formula, symbol and diagram: change no mathematics at all, not even an obvious slip;
- \scanpage and \mspage lines unchanged, in their places.
Translate the French words inside \deleted, \inserted, \margin and \unsure too. An \unsure{a|b} with alternative
readings: translate each alternative and keep the | between them (if two French alternatives give the same English,
still keep both). French words inside \text{...} or \mathrm{...} in formulas: translate them only when they are
ordinary words (e.g. \text{si} -> \text{if}); keep names of objects and notation as they are.
Mathematical terms: use the standard English terms (champ -> stack, catégorie fibrée -> fibred category,
topos, site, faisceau -> sheaf, gerbe -> gerbe, fibration, cofibration, équivalence faible -> weak equivalence,
modèle fermé -> closed model, etc.).

Answer in exactly this form, with nothing before the first marker:
=====BEGIN TARGET_NEW=====
(the complete English page)
=====END TARGET_NEW=====
=====NOTES=====
(readings you were unsure how to translate, with the French; or "none")

\scanpage{22}
\mspage{9}

Alternative presentation of theory, with possibly slightly less strong result --- as presentation of handy \unsure{ns} conditions on a $W$, so that there should exist a closed model structure on $\mathcal A$, s.th. $C=\text{mono}$, $W=$ the given one, hence $TC=C\cap W$, $F$ defined by \deleted{\unsure{lift}} RLP with respect to $TC=C\cap W$, \inserted{(say $(TC)_*$)} $TF$ (``Mono-injective'' maps) defined by RLP with respect to $C$.
\margin{$(TF=C_*)$}

The problems which remain (as we know \inserted{already} $(TF)^*=(C_*)^*=C$)

\textcircled{a}
\[
F^*=\deleted{\unsure{\text{any}}}((TC)_*)^*=TC
\]
--- and as \deleted{$\unsure{((TC)_*}$} $F^*\subset(TF)^*=C$, this amounts to: any monomorphism which has the LLP with respect to $F$ is in $W$. (A saturation type property of $W$ with respect to monomorphisms)

\textcircled{b} $TF=W\cap F$ --- in terms of the assumptions already made previously upon $W$, we know $TF\subset W$ i.e. $TF\subset W\cap F$, thus the problem is $W\cap F\subset TF$, i.e. any $f\in W$ which has the RLP with respect to $W\cap C$ is in $TF$ i.e. is Mono-injective.

c) Factorization $f=pi$ with either $p\in TF$, $i\in C$ (but this is already known and independent of $W$), or $p\in F$, $i\in TC$ \inserted{and even $i\in C\cap W$} --- and this shouldn't be too hard in terms of 3) and 4) by standard arguments. Thus I'll admit c for the time being.

\textcircled{d} Moreover, I'm interested in the following, quite important for me, dual to 3): If $f\in F:X-Y$, and $(Y'-Y)\in W$, then $(X'-X)\in W$.

For handling \textcircled{a} \textcircled{b} \textcircled{d} presumably I'll have to rely strongly upon factorization c). Thus for a), using factorization of $f=pi$, and using $f\in F^*$ we get a section $s$ of $p$ \deleted{\unsure{f}} s.th. $sf=i$, then $f$ is a retract of $i\in W$, and we win if we assume 5).

X\arrow[ur,hook,"i\in W\cap C"]\arrow[r,hook,"f"']&Y\arrow[u,bend right=55,"s"']
